title: Not by faith alone but also by works: conversion acts and growth
source_text: XXX. Quando vero docent nos, non sola fide, sed etiam per opera justificari, per id minime significatum volunt fideles bonis quibusdam operibus remissionem peccatorum suorum, proprie loquendo mereri, eamque non esse omnino gratuitam: sed hoc solum fidei actum, a spe, a fiducia, ab odio peccati, a dilectione Dei, distinctum & sejunctum, non esse unicam & solam conditionem, quam Deus a nobis exigit, ad hoc ut spiritus sanctificantis donum, & remissionem peccatorum nostrorum ab ipso consequamur. Neque ut salutaris istius gratiae participes fiamus, sufficere nudum assensum Evangelii verbo adhibitum, sed praeterea requiri peccati detestationem, novae vitae propositum, aliquos divinae dilectionis actus, spem veniae, & fiduciam in Deum, & si quae alia sint quibus constat vera ad Deum conversio. Ac praeterea hominem, quem gratia Christi semel justum reddidit, exercitio bonorum operum in justitia & sanctitate crescere, & acceptae justitiae, juxta divina promissa, recipere augmentum; quae omnia facile Protestantes concedunt, nec iis adversus illa pugnare est animus, quando cum Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae, de justificatione gratuita disputant.
pass_a_gloss: But when they teach that we are justified not by faith alone but also by works, by that they by no means wish it to be signified that the faithful properly speaking merit the remission of their sins by certain good works, and that it is not altogether gratuitous: but only this, that an act of faith distinct and separated from hope, from trust, from hatred of sin, from the love of God, is not the unique and sole condition which God requires of us in order that we may obtain from him the gift of the sanctifying Spirit and the remission of our sins. Nor, that we may become partakers of that saving grace, does a naked assent given to the word of the Gospel suffice, but there is required besides detestation of sin, a purpose of new life, some acts of divine love, hope of pardon, and trust in God, and whatever else constitutes true conversion to God. And besides, the man whom the grace of Christ has once made just grows by the exercise of good works in righteousness and holiness, and receives increase of the righteousness received, according to the divine promises; all which the Protestants easily concede, nor is it their mind to fight against those things when they dispute with the Doctors of the Roman Church about gratuitous justification.
pass_b_english: Roman not-faith-alone-but-works does not mean properly meriting remission.
Means: bare assent is not the sole condition—conversion acts needed; the justified grow by works—Protestants concede the substance.
